# Modifying Data {#modifydata}

Real-world data is messy. Customer databases have typos, survey exports come with weird column names, and someone always manages to sneak a text field into what should be a numeric column. This chapter is about reshaping, cleaning, and wrangling your data into something you can actually work with.

We cover both base R and tidyverse approaches here. Think of base R as the reliable sedan that has been around forever -- it gets the job done. The tidyverse is the newer model with better ergonomics and a cleaner dashboard. Both get you to the same destination; it is mostly a matter of preference and readability. For the full dplyr treatment, see Chapter \@ref(dplyr).

## Creating new variables

### Base R approach

Sometimes you need a variable that does not exist yet. Maybe you want total revenue (price times quantity), or a combined satisfaction score. In base R, you create new columns by assigning directly to the data frame using the `$` operator.

For example, if we wanted to create a variable in the `iris` dataset that was a sum of `Sepal.Length` and `Sepal.Width` and call it `Sepal.dimensions`:

```{r eval=FALSE}
iris$Sepal.dimensions <- iris$Sepal.Length + iris$Sepal.Width
```

There might be times when you want to overwrite an existing variable instead of creating a new one. In that case, just use the same variable name on the left side. Be careful with this -- there is no undo button.

```{r eval=FALSE}
iris$Sepal.Length <- iris$Sepal.Length + iris$Sepal.Width
```

### Tidyverse approach (dplyr)

The `mutate()` function from **dplyr** provides a cleaner way to create new variables. The big win here is readability -- you do not have to keep typing the data frame name over and over.

```{r eval=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
iris <- iris %>%
  mutate(Sepal.dimensions = Sepal.Length + Sepal.Width)
```

Note how `mutate()` does not require you to repeat the data frame name for each variable --- just use column names directly.



## Subsetting data and dropping factor levels

Subsetting is basically filtering out the noise. You have a big dataset and you only want the records that meet certain criteria -- customers who spent more than $100, survey respondents from a particular region, transactions from last quarter. This is one of the most common operations in any data analysis workflow.

### Base R approach

This creates a subset of `iris` such that `Sepal.Length` is greater than or equal to 5.8. Think of it as pulling only the high-value records.


```{r include=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
opts_chunk$set(echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE)
```


```{r}
irisSubset1 <- iris[iris$Sepal.Length >= 5.8,]
summary(irisSubset1$Sepal.Length)
```

You can also stack multiple conditions. Want customers who are both high-spending AND from a specific region? Same idea:

```{r}
irisSubset2 <- iris[iris$Sepal.Length >= 5.8 & iris$Sepal.Width < 3,]
summary(irisSubset2)
```

Subsetting based on a factor variable works a bit differently. The following line of code creates a subset of the `iris` dataset that has only two types of Species -- like filtering your CRM to show only two customer segments.

```{r}
irisSubset3 <- subset(iris, Species %in% c("setosa", "versicolor"))
# This can also be accomplished by the following statement
# irisSubset3 <- iris[iris$Species != "virginica",]
```

### Tidyverse approach (dplyr)

Here is the modern way. The `filter()` function from **dplyr** reads almost like plain English, which makes your code much easier to revisit six months later when you have forgotten what you were doing.

```{r}
irisSubset1_tidy <- iris %>% filter(Sepal.Length >= 5.8)
summary(irisSubset1_tidy$Sepal.Length)
```

```{r}
irisSubset2_tidy <- iris %>% filter(Sepal.Length >= 5.8, Sepal.Width < 3)
summary(irisSubset2_tidy)
```

```{r}
irisSubset3_tidy <- iris %>% filter(Species %in% c("setosa", "versicolor"))
```

Let us verify that we indeed have only two levels of the `Species` variable.

```{r}
summary(irisSubset3$Species)
```

Here is a gotcha that trips people up: even though we excluded `virginica`, R still remembers it existed as a factor level -- it just shows 0 observations. It is like deleting a department from your org chart but the label still shows up in the dropdown menu. To clean that up, we re-factor:

```{r}
irisSubset3$Species=factor(irisSubset3$Species)
```

Let us verify that did the trick.

```{r}
summary(irisSubset3$Species)
```



## Reordering factor levels

### Base R approach

Sometimes the default alphabetical ordering of factor levels does not match what you actually need. Maybe you want your customer satisfaction levels to go from "Very Unsatisfied" to "Very Satisfied" instead of alphabetical order. Here is how you take control.

```{r}
levels(iris$Species)
```

The default sequence is `setosa`, `versicolor`, and `virginica`. Let us reverse it -- because sometimes you want the premium tier listed first.

```{r}
iris$Species <- factor(iris$Species, levels(iris$Species)[c(3, 2, 1)])
```

By specifying the sequence, the earlier third level now becomes the first, the second stays put, and the old first level moves to third. Let us verify:

```{r}
levels(iris$Species)
```

### Tidyverse approach (forcats)

The **forcats** package (Chapter \@ref(forcats)) makes reordering factor levels feel less like a puzzle. The function names actually tell you what they do, which is a refreshing change.

```{r}
library(forcats)
# Reverse the levels
iris$Species <- fct_rev(iris$Species)
levels(iris$Species)
```

```{r}
# Set specific order
iris$Species <- fct_relevel(iris$Species, "setosa", "versicolor", "virginica")
levels(iris$Species)
```

## Reordering dataset entries

### Base R approach

Need to sort your data? Maybe you want to see your highest-revenue customers at the top, or sort survey responses by completion time. The `order` function is your friend here, even if it looks a bit cryptic at first.

For example, the `Sepal.Length` of the first row of the `iris` dataset:

```{r}
iris$Sepal.Length[1]
```

And the range of the variable:

```{r}
range(iris$Sepal.Length)
```

Sorting in ascending order (smallest to largest -- think of it as ranking from your lowest to highest spender):

```{r}
ascendingiris <- iris[order(iris$Sepal.Length),]
head(ascendingiris$Sepal.Length)
```

And descending order -- the "show me the top performers first" view:

```{r}
descendingiris <- iris[order(-iris$Sepal.Length),]
head(descendingiris$Sepal.Length)
```

### Tidyverse approach (dplyr)

The `arrange()` function is much more readable. You can practically read it as a sentence: "take this data and arrange it by this column."

```{r}
ascendingiris_tidy <- iris %>% arrange(Sepal.Length)
head(ascendingiris_tidy$Sepal.Length)
```

```{r}
descendingiris_tidy <- iris %>% arrange(desc(Sepal.Length))
head(descendingiris_tidy$Sepal.Length)
```


## Changing column names

Sometimes column names are terrible. Maybe they came from a database export with names like `X_VAR_007_Q3` or someone used spaces and special characters. Renaming them is a small investment that pays dividends in readability.

### Base R approach

Current names of columns in dataset:

```{r}
names(irisSubset3)
```

Rename the `Species` column:

```{r}
names(irisSubset3)[5] <- "SpeciesWithoutvirginica"
names(irisSubset3)
```


```{r eval=FALSE}
names(dataname) <- c("newcol1", "newcol2", "newcol3") # for a 3 column dataset
names(dataname)[3] <- "latestcol3name" # changing name for only the third column
```

### Tidyverse approach (dplyr)

The `rename()` function from **dplyr** uses a `new_name = old_name` syntax, which reads more naturally:

```{r eval=FALSE}
dataname <- dataname %>% rename(newnamecol1 = oldnamecol1, newnamecol2 = oldnamecol2)
```

Use `rename_with()` to apply a function to column names -- great for bulk cleanup:

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Make all column names lowercase
dataname <- dataname %>% rename_with(tolower)
```



## Renaming/Collapsing factor levels

Sometimes you need to relabel your categories. Maybe the marketing team decided "Premium" sounds better than "Tier 3," or you want to collapse several small segments into an "Other" bucket. Here is how to do it.

Let us make a copy of the iris dataset to experiment with:

```{r}
playiris=iris
levels(playiris$Species)
```

Pay attention to the order of the factor levels -- it matters for what comes next. We will change `virginica` to `factor3` and `versicolor` to `factor2` using two different approaches.

First approach -- match by name. This is the safer method because you are being explicit about which label you are changing:

```{r}
levels(playiris$Species)[levels(playiris$Species)=="virginica"]="factor3"
levels(playiris$Species)
```

Second approach -- match by position. This works but is riskier because if your factor levels ever change order, you will rename the wrong category. Proceed with caution.

```{r}
levels(playiris$Species)[2]="factor2"
levels(playiris$Species)
```

You can also rename all levels at once if you are feeling bold:

```{r}
levels(playiris$Species)=c("newlevel1","newlevel2","newlevel3")
levels(playiris$Species)
```

## Converting data types

OK, this section is admittedly a bit dry -- but it is one of those "eat your vegetables" topics. Getting your data types right is absolutely essential because half the errors you will encounter in R come down to R treating a variable as one type when you expected another. Five minutes here saves hours of confusion later.

### Factor to numeric

This comes in handy when you have a factor variable with numbers as values and you want to treat it as a numeric variable. Think of a survey where satisfaction ratings (1-5) got imported as categories instead of numbers. This discussion is [based on this Stack Overflow post.](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/3418128/how-to-convert-a-factor-to-an-integer-numeric-without-a-loss-of-information)

Let us go back to the `playiris` dataset. Remember the factor levels?

```{r}
levels(playiris$Species)
```

If we summarize the variable, it gives us the number of observations per level -- a count, not a statistical summary:

```{r}
summary(playiris$Species)
```

Let us convert the level labels to numbers:

```{r}
levels(playiris$Species)=c("1","2","3")
summary(playiris$Species)
```

Here is the important part. Even though the labels look like numbers now, R is still treating them as categories. It is still counting observations per group instead of computing a mean. R does not care what the labels look like -- it cares about the data type. To actually make the switch, you need to explicitly convert:

```{r}
playiris$Species=as.numeric(levels(playiris$Species))[playiris$Species]
# This can also be accomplished by the following.
# playiris$Species=as.numeric(as.character(playiris$Species))
```

Now if we summarize the variable, we get the real numeric summary -- min, max, mean, the works:

```{r}
summary(playiris$Species)
```


### Numeric to Factor - Binning variables

Let us re-convert the Species variable back to a factor:

```{r}
playiris$Species=factor(playiris$Species)
summary(playiris$Species)
```

Sometimes you need to go the other direction -- take a continuous number and turn it into categories. In business, this is incredibly common. Think "low / medium / high revenue customers" or "small / medium / large deal sizes." This process is called binning.

```{r}
summary(playiris$Petal.Length)
```

Our goal is to place all observations with `Petal.Length` at or below the 25th percentile (1.6) as "low" and those above the 75th percentile (5.1) as "high." Everything in between gets "medium." The `cut()` function does the heavy lifting:

```{r}
playiris$Petal.LengthFactor=cut(playiris$Petal.Length,breaks = c(1,1.6,5.1,6.9),labels = c("low","medium","high"),include.lowest = TRUE,ordered_result = TRUE)
```

Another approach uses nested `ifelse` statements -- a bit harder to read, but flexible:

```{r}
playiris$Petallength.Factor=ifelse(playiris$Petal.Length<=1.6,"low",ifelse(playiris$Petal.Length>5.1,"high","medium"))
```

Binning may also be needed to create equal interval bins and equal frequency bins. Please see [this response](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/42037740/equal-frequency-and-equal-width-binning-in-r) and [this response](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/5731116/equal-frequency-discretization-in-r/5741495#5741495) on Stack OVerflow for more details on the possible solutions.

### Factor and Numeric to Character and vice versa

There are times when you need your values as plain text -- maybe for string matching, text mining, or just to get a clean export. Converting between data types is like switching currencies: the value is the same, but the format matters for what you want to do with it.

Let us look at the structure of our playground dataset:
```{r}
str(playiris)
```

Convert `Species` and `Petal.LengthFactor` to character variables:

```{r}
playiris$Species=as.character(playiris$Species)
playiris$Petal.LengthFactor=as.character(playiris$Petal.LengthFactor)
str(playiris)
```

The results confirm our conversion worked. Converting them back to factors or numeric is straightforward -- just use the corresponding `as.*` function:

```{r}
playiris$Species=as.numeric(playiris$Species)
playiris$Petal.LengthFactor=as.factor(playiris$Petal.LengthFactor)
str(playiris)

```
